text:
elaine: Heads up — we're bringing in NeoMinimus (community v0.9) for benchmarking. License has a weird non-commercial+redistribute clause. Two quick questions: 1) Can we host inference behind Redwood API for paid customers? 2) Can we deliver a quantized on‑prem container to a customer who wants everything on their VPC?

elaine: Pasting the exact excerpt from LICENSE.md (emphasis mine):
```
Section 4.b Redistribution and Use: The Model Weights and any Derivative Works may not be redistributed for commercial purposes. Hosting the Model as an inference service is permitted only when the provider does not redistribute the Weights directly and does not offer a copy of the model to end users.
```

vikram (legal): Short answer: hosting via Redwood API is likely OK if the clause is interpreted literally — inference-as-a-service that never distributes weights to customers fits "does not redistribute the Weights directly". On‑prem container or shipping quantized binaries is risk — that looks like redistribution of Derivative Works. :warning:

vikram (legal): A couple of nuances: converting weights (quantization/pruning) creates a derivative in many jurisdictions; so a 4-bit converted file is not the original "Weights" and still falls under the redistribution restriction. Also the clause leaves ambiguity around "commercial purposes" — does our usage (paid customers) count? Almost certainly yes.

sanjay: So to be explicit: hosting in Redwood Hosted API == probably OK, Dedicated nodes we run for a customer in our cloud == probably OK, but handing over a Docker image that contains quantized weights == NOT OK, right?

vikram (legal): Correct on the spectrum. Hosted and Dedicated (where we control the infra and never hand over weight files) are defensible. On‑prem images or any package that includes the weights (even in quantized form) will likely breach the redistribution prohibition.

vikram (legal): Recommended mitigations:
- Ask upstream for a commercial license or an exception for redistribution to a named customer.
- If upstream declines, offer a "self-host proxy" pattern: provide a lightweight wrapper that calls our hosted endpoint (no weights included) — but remember that means traffic routes through our infra and we need a contract for SLA/costs.
- For Dedicated/Private deployments: only deploy if we can agree on a deployment model where weights remain under our control or under a contract that permits the customer to run the model in a managed way.

elaine: Attribution: the LICENSE has a short attribution line. Do we need to show the model name in the product UI or docs? The customer wants a white‑label experience.

vikram (legal): If the license mandates attribution, we should comply. The clause is usually explicit ("must display attribution in UI and docs"). If it's vague, negotiate: many model authors will allow removing visible branding in enterprise commercial deals in exchange for a fee or contract term.

licensing-bot: Internal checklist reminder: file intake -> add 'no‑redistrib weights' flag -> block onprem image build until legal clearance. Link: https://internal.redwood/ops/model-licensing (internal).

sanjay: Confirming one more thing — if we perform quantization in our runtime (on the fly in memory) and never write quantized weights to disk or deliver them, does that reduce risk?

vikram (legal): Lower risk but not zero. If the quantization is transient and never distributed, it's closer to permitted hosting. However, keep evidence that weights were never exported. Also flag telemetry/policy (audit logs) so we can prove compliance.

elaine: OK next steps: I'll open a licensing ticket to request a commercial redistribution carve‑out from the model authors for the specific customer. If no carve‑out, we proceed with hosted/Dedicated offering and decline on‑prem container. I'll update the onboarding checklist to block image builds for models with non‑redistrib clauses. :+1:

vikram (legal): Sounds good — ping me on the ticket and I can draft the request language and fallback contract language for the customer.

elaine: thanks all.
